cards.text: The war between the house of Saul and the house of David drags on, and on Saul's side, Abner keeps getting stronger. Abner is the commander of Saul's army, and he's the one who made Saul's son Ish-bosheth king (1 Samuel 14:50; 2 Samuel 2:8-9). Then Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with Rizpah, his father Saul's concubine.

cards.question: Ish-bosheth just accused the man who made him king. How does Abner take it?

cards.text: Abner fires back, "Am I the head of a dog that belongs to Judah?" When a man opens with THAT, friend, buckle up for a SPEECH.

cards.question: Abner reminds Ish-bosheth he's been loyal to Saul's house all this time. True or false: Abner says he has already handed Ish-bosheth over to David.

cards.text: Then Abner puts his own name on the line: "May God punish Abner, and ever so severely," if he doesn't do for David what the LORD has sworn to him.

cards.question: What does Abner swear he'll do for David?

answers.text: Bring the whole kingdom over to David
Split the land between both houses
Leave the war and go back home

cards.question: After Abner's oath, Ish-bosheth argues right back at him.

cards.text: For fear of Abner, Ish-bosheth doesn't dare say another word. I know that kind of quiet, friend, because I did YEARS of it in a junk drawer and got GOOD at it.
So Abner sends messengers to David with a question: "To whom does the land belong?" Then he makes David an offer.

cards.question: Abner says his hand will be with David to bring all Israel over. What does Abner ask David to make with him?

cards.text: David says good, he'll make the covenant. But there's one thing he requires, ONE, and Abner better not show his face without it.

cards.question: What does David require Abner to bring when he comes to see him?

cards.text: Then David sends messengers straight to Ish-bosheth: "Give me back my wife, Michal," the bride David paid Saul's price for back in the day (1 Samuel 18:25-27).

cards.question: Ish-bosheth refuses David's demand and keeps Michal away from him.

cards.text: Ish-bosheth sends and takes Michal from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish. And Paltiel follows her, weeping all the way to Bahurim.

cards.question: Paltiel is still following Michal, weeping. Who tells him to go back?

cards.text: Next, Abner sits down with the elders of Israel, and friend, listen to what comes out of his mouth: "In the past you sought David as your king."

cards.question: Abner tells the elders to take action now. What has the LORD said He will do through His servant David?

answers.text: Save Israel from the Philistines and all their enemies
Build a house for His name in Jerusalem
Lead Israel across the Jordan into a new land

cards.question: Abner doesn't stop with the elders. He also talks to Saul's own tribe (1 Samuel 9:1-2), the ___.

cards.text: Then Abner heads to Hebron to tell David everything that seemed good to Israel and the whole house of Benjamin. He shows up with twenty of his men.

cards.question: Abner, the commander from Saul's side of the war, arrives at Hebron with twenty men. What does David do?

answers.text: He holds a feast for them
He makes them wait outside the city

cards.question: Abner tells David he'll go gather all Israel to make a covenant with him. How does Abner leave Hebron?

cards.text: We'll set this batch on the cooling rack for now. But trust me, friend, this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: The joke compares Ish-bosheth's silence to Papa Dorin's quiet years in the drawer. Ish-bosheth goes quiet because he is afraid of Abner (2 Samuel 3:11). Papa Dorin went quiet because he had given up on himself, not because he feared anyone. The two actions don't match, so the comparison doesn't click.

rule.text: Find the core action in the fact: running away, waiting, being outnumbered, preparing, being surprised. The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Stop 2 has almost no humor. Across seven story cards there is only a mild emphasis on "ONE" (card 3) and "listen to what comes out of his mouth" (card 9). Several moments could hold a real laugh without muddying a fact: Abner switching sides and pitching David to the elders, Abner showing up at his former enemy's door with twenty men, and David answering with a feast. As written, most cards read like a nice dad being pleasant.

rule.text: Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The closing line "But trust me, friend, this story is NOT done" nearly copies the example line in the docs ("Trust me, friend, this story's not done"). It should be an original line.

rule.text: The examples show the idea. Write your own line each time.
